definition: A recursive transition network ("RTN") is a graph theoretical schematic used to represent the rules of a context-free grammar.
details: RTNs have application to programming languages, natural language and lexical analysis. Any sentence that is constructed according to the rules of an RTN is said to be "well-formed". The structural elements of a well-formed sentence may also be well-formed sentences by themselves, or they may be simpler structures. This is why RTNs are described as recursive.

explainer.lead: A graph-theoretical schematic for representing the rules of a context-free grammar. It matters as a formalism for defining well-formed structures in languages.

tiers.eli5: It's like a set of connected stepping stones: you follow a path to build a valid sentence, and some stones can loop back to let a piece contain smaller pieces of the same kind.
tiers.practitioner: Used for programming languages, natural language, and lexical analysis; the pitfall is that recursion lets structures nest, so well-formedness must be checked against the rules rather than assumed.
tiers.paperLevel: Defined as a graph theoretical schematic used to represent the rules of a context-free grammar; a sentence built according to its rules is well-formed, and structural elements of a well-formed sentence may themselves be well-formed sentences or simpler structures — which is why RTNs are called recursive.

explainer.example: An RTN for a clause can contain a nested clause as one of its structural elements, which is itself well-formed by the same rules.
